questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option D

👉 No Error.

📌 Rule / Concept: Subjunctive Mood with "As though" / "As if"

The conjunctions "as though" and "as if" are used to describe a hypothetical or imaginary situation. The tense used in the following clause depends on the relationship between the two actions:

Past Tense (Unreal Present): Used to describe a situation that is contrary to the present fact (e.g., He talks as though he were a king).

Past Perfect Tense (Unreal Past): Used when the hypothetical situation refers to a time prior to the action in the main clause. If the main verb is in the past tense (explained), the past perfect (had known) correctly indicates a hypothetical prior state.

Corrected Sentence: The officer explained the situation as though he had prior knowledge of every development in the case. (No correction required)

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: He behaves as if he owned the whole company. (Unreal present/general state)

Example 2: She looked as though she had seen a ghost. (Unreal past relative to the looking)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “cause” with “reason

Rule / Concept: Reason vs. Cause

1.Cause (Noun): Refers to the person, thing, or event that makes something happen (the origin/producer of an effect).

2.Preposition: Usually followed by "of".

3.Context: Used for physical or scientific results (e.g., the cause of the fire).

4.Reason (Noun): Refers to the justification, explanation, or motive for an action or belief.

5.Preposition: Usually followed by "for".

6.Context: Used for human logic, decisions, or excuses (e.g., the reason for his absence).

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the director is expected to provide an explanation or a justification for the sales performance to the board. This involves human analysis and logic rather than a direct physical trigger. Furthermore, the sentence uses the preposition "for". Since "cause" typically pairs with "of" to indicate a physical origin, and "reason" pairs with "for" to indicate an explanation, "reason" is the correct fit here.

More Examples for Clarity -

1. Scientists are studying the cause of the disease. (Physical origin)

2. There is no reason for you to be angry. (Justification)

3. The reason why he left is unknown.

options_en: Historical records indicate that the indigenous tribes of the valley
seldom if never migrated to the higher altitudes, preferring the fertile
plains that provided a steady supply of resources throughout the year.
No error
options_hi: Historical records indicate that the indigenous tribes of the valley
seldom if never migrated to the higher altitudes, preferring the fertile
plains that provided a steady supply of resources throughout the year.
No error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) . Replace “seldom if never” with “seldom if ever”.

Rule / Concept: Seldom if ever / Seldom or never

Seldom is a negative adverb. To maintain logical and grammatical consistency, it must be paired correctly to form a compound adverbial phrase. There are only two standard idiomatic combinations:

  1. Seldom if ever: Meaning "rarely, if at all."

  2. Seldom or never: Meaning "rarely or not at all."



Application to the Given Question

...seldom if never migrated to the higher altitudes...

The sentence uses the hybrid phrase "seldom if never," which is a violation of the rule. Since the conjunction "if" is used, it must be followed by "ever" to suggest a possibility. Alternatively, the sentence could have used "seldom or never," but based on the structure provided, "if ever" is the standard correction for this specific error type



More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 : He seldom or never goes to the gym despite paying for a premium membership. ✅

Example 2 : Such a rare celestial event is seldom if ever seen twice in a single lifetime. ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 : She seldom if never speaks in public meetings. ❌

Wrong example 2 : We seldom or ever visit our relatives in the countryside ❌

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

The Trap: Examiners often swap the endings (seldom if never / seldom or ever) to confuse students who are reading too quickly. Always pause when you see "seldom" to check the conjunction-adverb pair.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “him” with “his”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Possessive Case before a Gerund -

A Gerund is a verb ending in -ing that functions as a noun. Because it acts as a noun, the word that modifies it must be a possessive adjective (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) or a possessive noun (Ram's, Manager's).

In formal grammar, you aren't annoyed by the "person" (him); you are annoyed by the "action" (his arriving).

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "arriving" is a gerund acting as the object of the preposition "by." The manager isn't necessarily annoyed by the man himself, but specifically by the act of his arrival being late. Therefore, the objective pronoun "him" must be changed to the possessive adjective "his.

Corrected Sentence - The regional manager was understandably annoyed by his arriving late for the high-stakes client meeting without any prior notice.

More Examples for Clarity -

No Error
options_hi: Although the movie was very

No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “much disappointing” with “very disappointing”

Rule / Concept: Very vs. Much with Participles

  • Very + Present Participle (V1 + ing): When an adjective ends in -ing and describes the effect something has, use very.

  • Example: Very interesting, very boring, very exciting.

  • Much + Past Participle (V3): When an adjective is in the third form of the verb, use much.

  • Example: Much admired, much discussed, much criticized

VERY :- It is used with positive degrees of adj/adv . Generally it

qualifies present participles. It can't qualify a verb

MUCH:- It is used with comparative degrees of adj/adv. Generally it

qualifies past participles. It can qualify a verb

Application to the Given Question

"...the movie was very interesting , the climax was much disappointing ..."

  • "Interesting" is a present participle (V1 + ing), so "very" is used correctly.

  • "Disappointing" is also a present participle (V1 + ing). Therefore, using "much" is grammatically incorrect. It must be replaced with "very".

  • Corrected Sentence

Although the movie was very interesting, the climax was very disappointing for the audience

failed to offer a logical rational for the timing of their implementation,

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “rational” with “rationale”.

Rule/Concept: Rational vs. Rationale

Rational (Adjective): Refers to something based on or in accordance with reason or logic. It describes a person's behavior, a thought process, or a decision as being sensible and sane.

Rationale (Noun): Refers to the set of reasons or a logical basis for a particular belief or a course of action. It is the "why" behind a decision.

Application to the Given Question - ...failed to offer a logical rational for the timing...

In this sentence, the word follows the adjective "logical" and functions as the object of the verb "offer." We need a noun to represent the "underlying reason" or "justification" for the timing of the reforms. "Rational" is an adjective and cannot serve this purpose; therefore, the noun "rationale" must be used.

Corrected Sentence - While the proposed structural reforms seemed theoretically sound, the committee failed to offer a logical rationale for the timing of their implementation, leading to widespread skepticism among the labor union representatives.

More Examples for Clarity -

1. No rational person would jump from a moving train without a life-threatening reason.

2. The memo explained the economic rationale for the merger.

3. Please provide a written rationale for your choice of software.

subsidies, the peasantry of this drought-stricken region is still struggling
to repay the high-interest loans taken from local moneylenders.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (B).

Replace “is” with “are”.

Rule/Concept: Nouns Singular in Form but Plural in Meaning -

Certain collective nouns such as Peasantry, Gentry, Clergy, Poultry, Cattle, and Police - do not end in ‘s’, yet they represent a group or class of individuals. These nouns are always considered plural and must be followed by a plural verb. In this context, "Peasantry" refers to the class of small farmers or agricultural laborers as a whole. Although it appears singular in form (lacking an 's'), it refers to a collective group of people. Therefore, the singular auxiliary verb "is" is grammatically incorrect. It must be replaced with the plural verb "are" to achieve proper subject-verb agreement

Corrected Sentence - Despite the widespread implementation of several modern farming techniques and subsidies, the peasantry of this drought-stricken region are still struggling to repay the high-interest loans taken from local moneylenders.

LIST: Some nouns that look singular but are plural:- Cattle, Vermin, Police, Gentry, Peasantry, Children, People, Poultry, Cavalry, Clergy, Infantry etc.

questions.solution_en:

📌Rule/Concept: Confusing Verb Pairs (Rise vs. Raise) -

Rise (Intransitive): It means to move upward or increase on its own. It cannot take a direct object.

Forms: Rise (V1) - Rose (V2) - Risen (V3) - Rising (Gerund/V+ing).

Example: Smoke is rising from the chimney. (No object)

Raise (Transitive): It means to lift something or to increase something. It must have a direct object.

Forms: Raise (V1) - Raised (V2) - Raised (V3) - Raising (Gerund/V+ing).

Example: They are raising the flag. (Object: flag)

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, we are talking about an action performed by the government upon an object: "the prices of petrol." Since there is a clear direct object being increased, we cannot use the intransitive verb Rise. We must use the transitive verb Raise. Therefore, the gerund form should be Raising, not Rising.

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"I found the auditors checking the ledger for inconsistencies."
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the following sentence.

"I found the auditors checking the ledger for inconsistencies."
options_en: The auditors were found to be checking the ledger for inconsistencies.
The auditors were found checking the ledger for inconsistencies by me.
The ledger was found being checked by the auditors.
The auditors were found to check the ledger.
options_hi: The auditors were found to be checking the ledger for inconsistencies.
The auditors were found checking the ledger for inconsistencies by me.
The ledger was found being checked by the auditors.
The auditors were found to check the ledger.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

📌 Rule / Concept: Verb + Object + V-ing (Perception / Discovery) – Passive Formation

When the active structure is: Subject + found + object + V-ing, the passive form becomes: Object + was/were + found + to be + V-ing. The infinitive marker “to be” is generally inserted before the -ing form in formal passive constructions. The tense (simple past) must remain unchanged.

📌 Application to the Given Question

I found the auditors checking the ledger for inconsistencies. Here, “found” is in the simple past tense and is followed by object + V-ing (“the auditors checking”). In passive voice, “the auditors” becomes the subject. The correct structure is: were + found + to be + checking. Hence, “The auditors were found to be checking the ledger for inconsistencies” is correct. Option (B) omits “to be,” making it less standard in formal grammar. Option (C) forms an awkward and incorrect structure (“being checked”). Option (D) changes the meaning by removing the continuous sense.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

For “found + object + V-ing,” use “was/were found to be + V-ing” in passive. Maintain the tense. Preserve the continuous sense when present in the original sentence. Avoid dropping necessary infinitive markers in formal constructions.

from the additional insights shared by the professor.
No error

highly informative, and most of the class benefited
from the additional insights shared by the professor.
No error.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) – replace “most of the class benefited” with “only they benefited”.

Concept: Few / A Few / The Few

Few → Almost none; emphasizes scarcity (negative sense)

A few → Some; emphasizes presence (positive sense)

The few → A specific small group; emphasizes a definite limited number

When the few is used, it refers only to that small, specific group. Saying “most of the class benefited” incorrectly extends the scope beyond the few.

Application to the Given Question -

Here, “the few students” is a specific small group.

Saying “most of the class benefited” contradicts the meaning, because only the few students attended and benefited.

Corrected Sentence - The few students who attended the special lecture found it highly informative, and only they benefited from the additional insights shared by the professor.

More Examples for Clarity -

The few employees who worked overtime received appreciation.

The few people present at the meeting understood the changes.

The few volunteers who arrived early helped organize the event.

Incorrect Usage -

The few students attended, but everyone in the class passed.

The few workers completed the task, and all employees praised them.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) – Remove AS.

📌 Rule / Concept: Superfluous use of 'As'

Certain verbs, known as Factitive Verbs, serve to show how an object is being defined, named, or elected. These verbs—including Name, Call, Elect, Appoint, Make, Choose, and Consider—take an object and an object complement directly.

In formal English, using the conjunction "as" between the object and the complement is grammatically redundant because the verb itself already establishes the relationship of "in the capacity of" or "identity."

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "the newly discovered reef" is the object, and "'The Sapphire Wall'" is the name being given to it (the complement). The verb "named" connects these two directly. Adding "as" is a common spoken error that is strictly penalized in SSC/Banking examinations. The sentence should transition directly from the object to the name.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: The team elected him captain for the upcoming season. (Not: as captain)

Example 2: I consider him a brother. (Not: as a brother)

Example 3: The Queen anointed him her successor. (Not: as her successor)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

👉 Replace “_____” with “were”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Second Conditional — Unreal Present (If-Clause Focus)

The Second Conditional is used to express a hypothetical, unreal, or unlikely situation in the present and its probable result.

Core structure:

If + past simple / were → would + base verb

 

  • The past form in the if-clause does not show past time.
  • It signals distance from reality.

💢 Application to the Given Question -

“If the dataset ______ more representative…”

The sentence does not claim that the dataset is currently representative.
It imagines a hypothetical improvement.

This is confirmed by the main clause:

“…it would enable the model…”

The presence of would automatically requires an unreal condition in the if-clause.

Therefore:

 

  • were → correctly marks an unreal present condition
  • is → wrongly treats the condition as real
  • has been → introduces present perfect (time reference not intended)
  • had been → wrongly shifts to unreal past (Third Conditional)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

Replace “which” with “that”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Relative Pronouns for Mixed Antecedents

When a sentence has two antecedents joined by "and"—where one is a human being (person) and the other is an animal or a non-living thing—we cannot use "who" (reserved for humans) or "which" (reserved for things/animals). In such specific cases, the relative pronoun "that" must be used as a neutral coordinator to refer to both simultaneously.

In this sentence, the relative pronoun refers to two distinct subjects: "The elderly gentleman" (a person) and "the vintage car" (an object). Using "which" incorrectly excludes the gentleman, and using "who" would incorrectly include the car. Therefore, "that" is the only grammatically correct option to represent both antecedents.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: The farmer and his ox that were working in the field were struck by lightning.

Example 2 ✅: We saw the actress and her jewelry that were the talk of the town.

Example 3 ✅: The pilot and the aircraft that went missing have finally been located.
